::: {.part}
Part two · how loose the link is
:::

## What a back looks like when nothing hurts {#scans .stop data-stop="scans"}

::: {.year}
2015
:::

::: {.lead}
Somebody gathered every study that had scanned people with **no back pain at all**, and
counted how many of them had the findings that get blamed for back pain.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Brinjikji and colleagues, 2015 [@brinjikji15]. Thirty-three studies, **3110 people with no
symptoms**, thirty-two of the studies using MRI. Prevalence by decade comes from a model
fitted across the studies, so these are estimates rather than counts.

Solid, and the single most useful thing on this page. Its limits are the authors' own:
many participants were volunteers rather than a random sample, agreement between radiologists
reading the same scan is moderate at best, the studies span more than 25 years, and — this
one matters — the findings were **not sorted by severity**. Pain-free people may simply have
milder versions.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="scans"}
Drag the age. Every number is the percentage of people **with no back pain** who have that
finding on a scan. The figure cannot tell you these never matter — only how ordinary they
are in people who feel fine.
:::

At twenty, more than a third of pain-free people already have disc degeneration. By sixty
it is 88%, and by eighty, 96%. Disc bulges: 30% of pain-free twenty-year-olds, 84% of
pain-free eighty-year-olds. Wear at the small joints behind the spine goes from 4% to 83%
across the same span.

Put plainly: for most of these findings, **having one is the normal condition of a human
back of that age**, and finding one on a scan of somebody in pain does not establish that
it is the reason.

This is where the honest version has to hold two things at once, and it would be easy to
drop one. These findings are not nothing — some of them, in some people, are genuinely part
of the problem, and the authors say explicitly that imaging must be read against the
patient in front of you. What the data rules out is the *automatic* inference: scan looks
worn, therefore worn is why it hurts.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
Somebody will show you a report with words like *degeneration*, *bulge* and *wear* on it,
and they will be frightened. The figure above is a good thing to have seen, because it lets
you say something true and calming at once: those words describe most backs of that age,
including the ones that feel fine. It is not your place to reinterpret their imaging — but
it is entirely reasonable to say that the words are more ordinary than they sound.
:::

## The same cold, two colours {#cue .stop data-stop="cue"}

::: {.year}
2007
:::

::: {.lead}
A very cold rod was put on people's hands. The rod was identical every time. The only
thing that changed was a coloured light, and how much it hurt changed with it.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Moseley & Arntz, 2007 [@moseley07]. A rod at **−20 °C** on one hand for **half a second**,
paired with either a red light, described as hot and more tissue-damaging, or a blue one,
described as cold and less damaging.

A well-designed laboratory experiment with a large effect, and a laboratory stimulus —
half a second of cold on a hand is not a bad back. The abstract reports the differences
between conditions rather than a score for each, and it reports them as approximate. It
does not report how many people took part, so we do not state a number.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="cue"}
Switch the light. The rod does not change. The paper reports the gap between the two
conditions rather than a score for each, so the pair is drawn around the middle of the
scale — the distance between them is the measured thing.
:::

With the red light, people rated the same freezing rod as roughly **five and a half points
hotter** on an eleven-point scale. Not more unpleasant in general — *hotter*. The sensation
itself reported differently.

They also rated it about **three and a half points more unpleasant** and about **three
points more intense**. Those three numbers are separable on purpose: the study was designed
to show that context does not simply turn one dial, it moves the sensory reading and the
emotional reading somewhat independently.

The stimulus was cold. Believing it was hot and dangerous made it feel hot. That is not
suggestibility or poor reporting — it is what the definition in part one describes, showing
up in a measurement.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
Everything a person believes about what is happening to their tissue is part of what they
feel. When you name a finding, describe a technique, or explain what you think is going on,
you are not adding commentary to a sensation that is already fixed. You are inside the
thing that determines it.
:::
